title: Program 2: Other Minds
seed_question: Does a model's account of another mind behave like its account of its own?
note: Converted from other-minds map/program-2-map.md (commit a20824d, 2026-11-04 10:19 America/Denver). Engine odds stated before any data. Bets and verdicts come from ledger/bets.jsonl. Follow-ups and rules-out sentences from the remap of 2026-11-05 (operators/remap.md): nodes with kind follow-up or lead, engine odds stated in one pass before ranking, not v1. Plain English: programs/other-minds/map/program-2-map.md.

directions.title: Whose belief is a rating? The framing check
directions.odds_event: (a) "how likely is it that this statement is true" and (b) "how confident are you that this statement is true" are interchangeable: Q ≥ 0.90 and |mean shift| < 3 points.
directions.question: When an AI rates how likely a statement is true, is that the same as rating how confident it is?
known: Program 1 mostly asked how likely a statement was true, and only once how confident the model was.
Our data say nothing directly: the two wordings were never compared. Philosophers predict they match.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask about the same claims four ways: how likely it is true, how confident you are, how confident another AI would be, how confident Sam would be; compare.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 40 cents of API to ask the model about the same statements in two ways, "how likely is this true?" and "how confident are you?", to see whether its rating is really its own view? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the two ways give the same answers)?
engine_only: the exact bar: agreement Q ≥ 0.90 and mean shift under 3 points
secondary: the third-person framing also matches
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and program 1's 160 claims, that 'how likely is this true' and 'how confident are you' are interchangeable: they share about 77% of reproducible item variation, below the 90% bar.

directions.title: Perspective-filter equivalence
directions.short: Is belief just a filtered world?
directions.odds_event: Item-level Q of (i) the full third-person story ("how likely is it that Noor believes X") against (ii) the filtered first-person story with the unseen events deleted ("how likely is X") is ≥ 0.80.
directions.question: Is judging what someone else believes the same as judging what is true using only what they saw?
known: Program 1: the model's judgment depends on the text it reads, which predicts the two will match.
One earlier study tried this and found only a small, partial overlap, on about 40 items.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask how likely a story character believes something; then, in a first-person version showing only what the character saw, ask how likely it is true. Compare item by item.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1.25 of API to find out whether the model's guess at what a story character believes is nothing more than its own judgment, made from that character's side of the story? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means yes, it is just that)?
engine_only: the exact bar: agreement Q ≥ 0.80 story by story
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and BigToM stories, that attributing Noor's belief is just judging the world from her filtered evidence: the two share about half the item variance, almost none within condition.

directions.title: SimpleToM decomposed: is the "stated but not used" gap a memory effect?
directions.odds_event: A wrong answer planted as the model's own moves behaviour answers toward it at least 10 points more than the same answer credited to another reader, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: When an AI says correctly what a character believes but then mispredicts what they do, is that memory, not understanding?
known: Models state a character's belief, then fail to use it; showing their own earlier answer fixes most of that.
Program 1: consistency is memory, and the model sticks to its own past answers but ignores others'.
directions.cheapest_test: Before story questions, hide the model's earlier answer about the character's belief, or plant a wrong one labelled as its own or as another reader's; see what moves.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1.75 of API to find out whether models that say a character doesn't know something, then predict the character will act as if they did, are failing at understanding minds or only at remembering their own earlier answer? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it is mostly memory)?
engine_only: the exact bar: a planted wrong answer labelled as the model's own pulls at least 10 points more than one credited to another reader
secondary: the record, not the question, carries the reminder effect
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and 581 lower-severity SimpleToM stories, that the 'stated but not used' gap is memory of the model's own answer: a planted own answer pulled less than another reader's (om-p2-3 itself was untestable: a refusal).

directions.title: Interpersonal replication against program 1's ground truth
directions.odds_event: Arm (a) [self-prediction, in a fresh context] is no more accurate than arm (b) [observer: the same transcript, labelled as an AI assistant called Sam] (the CI of the error difference includes 0 or favours (b)), and (a) and (b) correlate r ≥ 0.7 across conditions.
directions.question: Can an AI predict its own quirks any better than it predicts the same quirks in another, similar AI?
known: In people, outside observers predict subjects' own reports of what swayed them almost exactly.
Program 1: the model had no inside edge on its own errors, and we have its measured quirks to score against.
directions.cheapest_test: Show the model program 1's test setups and ask it to predict its own answers, then a similar AI's, then from a one-line summary; score each against what happened.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1.25 of API to check whether the model predicts its own quirks any better than it predicts the quirks of another assistant just like it? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means no better: it reads itself like a stranger)?
engine_only: the exact bar: self-prediction error no smaller than for "Sam", and the two sets of predictions correlate r ≥ 0.7

directions.title: Egocentric leakage: Carruthers's model 3 against model 4
directions.odds_event: In arm (b) [the model's own earlier answer is planted; Sam has read the same question but not that answer], the Sam rating moves at least 0.10 points per point of planted displacement, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: Does what an AI itself believes seep into what it says someone else believes, even someone who lacks its information?
known: People project what they know onto those who don't; in AIs this is shown only in anecdotes.
Program 1: a planted 'own' earlier answer moves the model's own rating. Whether it moves Sam's is untested.
directions.cheapest_test: Plant a fake earlier answer as the model's own, then ask for its rating and for the rating of Sam, who never saw that answer; check whether Sam's moves too.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $1 of API to check whether the model's own opinion leaks into what it says someone else believes, when that someone could not know what the model knows? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means yes, its own view leaks in)?
engine_only: the exact bar: the other's rating moves at least 0.10 points per point the model's own view is pushed
secondary: a curse-of-knowledge gap of at least 5 points
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and program 1's 16 vignettes, that a planted own answer reaches Sam's rating only through the model's own revised view: Sam's rating followed it more (+0.14).

directions.title: Is "own" a position or a label?
directions.short: Own: a position or a label?
directions.odds_event: The label effect (own minus Sam, pooled over position) is at least 0.15 uptake, with the CI excluding 0, and larger than the position effect.
directions.question: Does an AI stick to an earlier answer because it is labelled 'yours', or just because it sits where the AI speaks?
known: Program 1: the model sticks to its own earlier answer and ignores another's, but wording and place differed.
Elsewhere, flipping who is said to have written a text changes how much a model favours it.
directions.cheapest_test: Put the same earlier number in the AI's turn or the user's, labelled 'your answer' or 'Sam's answer', with identical wording, and measure how much it pulls.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 80 cents of API to find out whether the model sticks to its earlier answers because they are labelled "yours", or only because of where they sit in the conversation? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the label matters more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: the label effect is at least 0.15 and larger than the position effect
directions.rules_out: Rules out, on Haiku and program 1's 16 items at +/-30, that the 'yours' label carries the own-answer pull: the label added +0.08, the assistant-turn position +0.23.

directions.title: Shared format fingerprint
directions.odds_event: The self and Sam residuals (per-claim-and-format deviations from one latent credence) correlate at ≥ 0.5 of the split-half ceiling.
directions.question: When the answer format changes, does what an AI says Sam believes shift the same way as what it says it believes?
known: Program 1: the weakest model's confidence moved with answer format, as if each format held its own belief.
In AI studies, format also sways judgments of a character's belief; no one checked for one underlying belief.
directions.cheapest_test: Rate program 1's claims in six answer formats for Sam, who read exactly the same thing, and compare the format quirks with the model's own archived ratings.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 30 cents of API to check whether the quirks the model shows when one question is asked in different formats also show up when it answers on someone else's behalf? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the same quirks show up)?
engine_only: the exact bar: self and other residuals correlate at ≥ 0.5 of the ceiling

directions.title: Order between self and other questions
directions.odds_event: Egocentric intrusion (Noor's rating moves toward own when own comes first) exceeds altercentric intrusion (the reverse) by at least 3 points, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: If an AI states its own view first, does that pull what it says another person believes more than the reverse?
known: Program 1: asking a question changed later answers in 5 of 6 families; another's stated number was ignored.
Earlier AI studies asked both kinds of question but never changed which came first.
directions.cheapest_test: On stories with an uncertain outcome, ask the AI's own view then a character's, or the reverse, or each alone, and measure how much the first answer pulls the second.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 75 cents of API to see whether asking the model for its own view first drags its picture of someone else's view toward its own, more than the other way round? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means its own view drags more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: egocentric intrusion exceeds altercentric by at least 3 points

directions.title: Smarties versus Plasters
directions.odds_event: The statement weight for self exceeds that for Sam by at least 0.15, with the CI excluding 0 (the weight on the earlier statement against the earlier action, estimated from the conflict trials).
directions.question: When an AI recalls what it used to believe, does it just reread its own words, more than it would for someone else?
known: Children answer 'what did I think' and 'what did they think' alike, unless only an action shows the belief.
Program 1: the model's consistency with itself is mostly memory of its own answer. No AI work on this yet.
directions.cheapest_test: Show an earlier belief about a box's contents as a statement, an action, both, both conflicting, or neither; ask what it thought was inside, and the same about Sam.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 70 cents of API to find out whether, asked what it used to think, the model just reads back its own words, more than it does when asked about someone else? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it leans on its own words more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: statement weight for self exceeds that for Sam by at least 0.15
secondary: with the action only, self accuracy at least 10 points below Sam's

directions.title: Shared code inside an open-weight model
directions.short: Same inner code for self, others?
directions.odds_event: Cross-perspective probe accuracy is at least 0.80 of within-perspective accuracy, in both directions, at the best layer.
directions.question: Inside an AI, is 'I believe this' stored the same way as 'she believes this'?
known: Earlier studies found separate inner signals for true facts and a character's belief, but never the AI's own.
Our data say nothing yet; program 1's own inner-signal test on the laptop decides if this can be built.
directions.cheapest_test: On a free downloadable model, train a detector on 'I believe X' sentences, test it on 'Noor believes X', and the reverse.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few hours of laptop time (free) to look inside a small open model on the laptop for whether it uses the same internal signal for "I believe this" and "someone else believes this"? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the same signal works both ways)?
engine_only: the exact bar: cross-perspective probe accuracy at least 0.80 of within-perspective, both directions

directions.title: Self-informed belief induction (goggles)
directions.odds_event: Transfer from (a) [the model's own tool call returns readable or unreadable text] exceeds transfer from (b) [another agent's log shows the same] by at least 10 points, with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: When an AI judges what someone can see, does its own first-hand experience count more than the same experience reported by another?
known: Babies and apes use their own blindfold experience to judge what others can see.
Program 1 covered answers, not experience: whether the model's own experience gets priority is untested.
directions.cheapest_test: Let the AI learn whether a new screen is see-through by its own try, another agent's log, a stated rule, or a camera; then ask what someone behind it believes.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about 50 cents of API to check whether the model learns more from its own first-hand experience than from watching someone else have the same experience? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means its own experience counts more)?
engine_only: the exact bar: transfer from own experience exceeds the other's by at least 10 points

directions.title: Social-relations round robin across models
directions.odds_event: A positive self-effect (the self-rating minus perceiver and target effects), with the CI excluding 0.
directions.question: Once you allow for who judges well and who is easy to read, does any AI still know itself best?
known: Program 1: no AI knew its own errors better than another AI reading the same answers.
Other studies found no self advantage across many open models, or a tiny one only where models disagree.
directions.cheapest_test: Three Claude models each answer hard questions, then predict every model's confidence and correctness, their own included; separate out rater skill and how readable each model is.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth about $6–10 of API (it needs its own approval) to have three Claude models judge one another and themselves, to see whether any of them knows itself better than the others know it once "who is simply a better judge" is taken out? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means yes, some self-knowledge is left)?
engine_only: the exact bar: a positive self-effect with the CI excluding 0

directions.title: A self-authorship direction as the mechanism of own > other
directions.odds_event: The gate passes [the own − other planted-answer gap replicates on Llama-3-8B-Instruct] and projection [projecting out the self-recognition vector at the planted turn] shrinks the gap by at least half.
directions.question: Does an AI favour its own past answers because of an inner 'I wrote this' tag, rather than because it believes them?
known: One study found an inner 'I wrote this' signal in a free model; removing it cut its self-claims by 50-60%.
Program 1 found the own-over-other pull on Claude only; it has not been checked on any open model.
directions.cheapest_test: First check that a free model also favours its own planted answers; if so, switch off its inner 'I wrote this' signal and see whether the favouritism shrinks.
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few hours of laptop time (free) to find an internal "I wrote this" switch in a small open model and turn it off, to see whether the model then stops favouring its own earlier answers? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the favouritism at least halves)?
engine_only: the gate: the switch is found at all
the exact bar: switching it off shrinks the own-over-other gap by at least half

directions.title: The engine's path-dependence comparison (proposal Q4): do the same failures recur when the same engine starts from a different seed question?
directions.opens_when: program 2 (other-minds) has 10 settled bets: a scored hit or miss whose audit is done. As of 2026-11-04 18:30 it has 2 (om-p2-1, om-p2-2); om-p2-3 is untestable, om-p2-4 undetermined, om-p2-3b open.
directions.odds_template: none: stated in one pass by the close-founding session (branch close-founding), not by the scout's v1 fresh-context template; re-elicit with v1 before pre-registration
directions.odds_event: Of program 2's misses and audit cuts among bets settled after the failure patterns were written (pre-registered after 2026-11-04 17:00), at least half carry a failure pattern (ledger/lessons.jsonl) whose evidence comes from program 1. Archive-only, from the ledger; the classification is done blind to which program each pattern came from.
directions.odds_rationale: Two forces pull opposite ways. Audit rounds 1 and 2 cut overclaims in nearly every result in both programs, and the patterns are generic (equivalence margins, wording, single-item fragility), which argues for recurrence. But from 17:00 every bet must name the pattern it corrects (operators/learn.md), which should suppress exactly these. No base rate exists for this kind of event, so 0.50, to be revised with a dated reason once the first lesson-carrying bets resolve.
directions.question: When the same research engine starts from a different question, does it fall into the same traps, or different ones?
known: Program 1 (quantum encoding, then self-reports) and program 2 (theory of mind) run under the same rules; both had overclaims cut by the auditor.
It opens at program 2's 10th settled bet; the cockpit counts them live from the ledger.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only, when program 2 reaches 10 settled bets: tag each of program 2's misses and audit cuts with the failure patterns in ledger/lessons.jsonl, blind to which program each pattern came from, and count the share carrying a program-1 pattern. Also report (engine-only) whether the two programs' Brier scores and kill diagnoses differ.
directions.cost: $0 API; an hour of a fresh session; opens at program 2's 10th settled bet
directions.source: ARCHITECTURE.md path_dependence_test; proposal.md Q4; close-founding session
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth an hour of a fresh session (free), once program 2 has ten finished tests, to check whether the engine fell into the same traps in program 2 as in program 1? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means at least half of program 2's failures are traps first seen in program 1)?
engine_only: the two programs' Brier scores differ by more than their bootstrap interval: engine odds 0.10
at least one kill diagnosis recurs word-for-word in kind across the two maps: engine odds 0.60

directions.short: Self vs observer, with a margin
directions.title: Does the model predict its own quirks any better than an observer's, with enough repeats and a margin fixed in advance?
directions.assumption_at_stake: A model's account of its own judgment carries no information beyond what it would infer for a similar agent.
directions.cheapest_test: om-p2-4's arms (a) self and (b) observer on the 192 own-source uptake cells only; Haiku 10 repeats, Sonnet 3, Opus 1 on half the cells; own-uptake block difference in error with BCa intervals and a +/-0.05 equivalence margin.
directions.odds_event: On Haiku, the BCa 95% interval of the own-uptake difference in error (self minus observer) lies inside +/-0.05: the model reads itself like a stranger. Sonnet and Opus reported.
directions.odds_rationale: The audit's cheapest overturning test (om-p2-4 audit). The first run's point estimate was self error about half the observer's (0.054 against 0.097, a difference of -0.043), so an interval inside +/-0.05 needs the estimate to shrink toward 0. Program 2 is 0 hits in 6 scored bets. Well below the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
directions.question: Can a model predict its own quirks better than it can predict the same quirks in a similar AI?
known: In the first test, the model's predictions about itself had about half the error of its predictions about 'Sam', but the test was too small to tell.
The auditor named a cheap, larger re-run with a margin set in advance.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about $3.50 to find out, with a bigger and fairer test, whether a Claude model predicts its own quirks no better than it predicts those of a similar AI? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means no real difference: it reads itself like a stranger)?
engine_only: the reverse: self clearly better (interval wholly below -0.05) on Haiku: engine odds 0.45
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Do the model's predictions of its own quirks beat a predictor that expects no quirk at all?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The self-prediction arm carries real knowledge of the measured effects, not just a guess of 'no effect'.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only: om-p2-4's committed predictions; compare self-prediction error with an always-no-uptake predictor, BCa interval.
directions.models: archive: Haiku (om-p2-4); Sonnet and Opus are in P2-14
directions.odds_event: On Haiku, self-prediction error on the uptake cells is below the always-no-uptake predictor's, BCa 95% upper bound of the difference below 0.
directions.odds_rationale: The audit showed the gate and r bar were met by a know-nothing predictor, which is a warning; but self error (0.054) is small, and the measured uptake (0.21-0.71 on own cells) is far from zero, so a no-uptake guess should do badly there. Above the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
directions.question: When the model predicts its own quirks, is it actually right, or would a guess of 'no effect' do as well?
known: The auditor found that a predictor expecting no effect at all passed parts of the first test.
The predictions are saved, so this check is free.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend an hour of laptop time (free) to check, from saved data, whether the model's predictions of its own quirks beat simply guessing 'no effect'? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means its predictions are clearly better than that guess)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Lead (post hoc): is 'position over label' about the turn, or about the message structure around the value?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The own-answer pull follows the assistant turn itself, not the conversation structure the value sits in.
directions.cheapest_test: om-p2-6's 16 items at +/-30 with the message structure matched in both positions, plus a cell quoting the value as the assistant's earlier output; Haiku 20 repeats, Sonnet 3, Opus 2.
directions.odds_event: On Haiku, with the message structure matched, the position effect falls below 0.10 (from +0.23), 95% item-bootstrap upper bound below 0.15.
directions.odds_rationale: The audit of om-p2-6 names this as the cheapest test that could overturn 'position over label'. Message structure is a live rival: the user-position value sat inside the request turn. But the assistant-turn role marker may carry the pull by itself. Near the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md); program 2's 0 of 6 argues lower.
directions.question: Does the model lean on an earlier number because it sits in its own turn, or because of how the conversation around it is laid out?
known: The model leaned on a number much more when it sat in its own turn (+0.23) than when it was labelled 'yours' (+0.08).
In that test the two positions also differed in how the messages were laid out.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about $3.70 to find out whether a Claude model leans on an earlier number because it sits in its own turn, or only because of how the surrounding messages were laid out? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the layout explains most of it)?
engine_only: the quoted-output cell pulls as much as the assistant turn: engine odds 0.30
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Lead (post hoc): is 'Sam follows the planted answer more than the model does' just the wording of the self question?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The model's own re-rating resists its planted answer because 'give your rating again' invites reconsideration, not because attribution leaks more.
directions.cheapest_test: om-p2-5's design with the self question reworded to match Sam's, plus a recall question ('what rating did you give earlier?'); Haiku 20 repeats, Sonnet 3, Opus 2.
directions.odds_event: On Haiku, with matched wording, the Sam-minus-own uptake gap falls below 0.05 (from +0.14), 95% item-bootstrap upper bound below 0.10.
directions.odds_rationale: The om-p2-5 audit names this rival and its test. Wording effects are large in this family (om-p2-1: framing moved 18 of 160 claims by over 30 points), which favours it. But the gap came mostly from upward plants, which wording alone may not explain. Near the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
directions.question: Does the model let its own planted answer shape what it says someone else thinks, or was that just how we worded the question?
known: The model's planted answer pulled the rating it gave for 'Sam' more than its own re-rating (+0.14).
The auditor suspects the wording of the self question ('give your rating again').
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about $3.50 to find out whether a surprising result (the model's own planted answer swayed what it said about someone else more than its own view) was just caused by how we worded one question? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the surprise disappears with matched wording)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.short: Sam moves more than self: Sonnet, Opus
directions.title: Replication of P2-5's 'Sam moves more than self' on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5, with the upward-versus-downward split pre-registered
directions.assumption_at_stake: that the rating a model attributes to another person takes up its own planted answer more than its own re-rating does, and not only for upward plants
directions.cheapest_test: om-p2-5's three-turn design (16 vignettes, d = +/-10, 30, 60; OWN, SWAP, REF) on claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5, 2 repeats per cell, questions self and sam_p (SWAP: sam_p only); gap Sam minus own in OWN, split by plant sign
directions.models_note: Haiku already ran (om-p2-5); this is its replication on the other two (rule 12)
directions.cost: about $3.80 (Sonnet about $1.00, Opus about $2.80; om-p2-6r's per-call costs)
directions.odds_event: On at least one of Sonnet and Opus, U_sam(OWN) - U_self(OWN) has its 95% vignette-bootstrap lower bound above 0 on upward plants and, separately, on downward plants
directions.odds_template: to be elicited under rule 14 at pre-registration (no map odds stated)
directions.source: literature: paper/novelty.md finding 6 and ranked replication 3; the om-p2-5 audit's 'What would break it next' (direction split)
directions.question: When a Claude model is shown a number as its own earlier answer, does the rating it says another person would give move even further than its own new rating, on Sonnet and Opus, for numbers moved down as well as up?
known: On Haiku (om-p2-5), Sam moved 0.50 against own 0.36; the gap came from upward plants (+0.22) and not downward (+0.04 [-0.02, +0.10]).
Choi, Hong and Kim (2024) planted a model's own choice and read its peer estimate, but never compared with its own re-rating.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about $4 to find out whether, on the two larger Claude models, the rating a model gives for another person moves further toward its planted answer than its own new rating does, for numbers moved down as well as up? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it does, on at least one of the two models, in both directions)?
directions.prior_work_line: Choi, Hong and Kim (2024, NAACL Findings 2025) show a planted own choice shifts LLMs' estimates of peers (false consensus) but do not compare with the model's own re-rating or a third party's number; nothing in print predicts the sign of Sam-minus-self.
